name: Oman
summary_text: Oman is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — and uniquely in the Gulf, combines an explicit anti-trans statute with a documented trans-traveler abuse case. The 2018 Penal Code criminalises "imitating the opposite sex" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, extending to foreign nationals. Enforcement is documented: in January 2018 the Royal Oman Police publicly announced arresting transgender women in Salalah after private-party photos circulated on social media; HRW documented arrests and convictions under the provision. Most concretely for travelers: in February 2024, Nin Kala, an Indian non-binary model and designer arriving at Muscat airport on a tourist visa, was pulled aside while their friends cleared immigration, taken to a private room, forced to remove their shirt, touched inappropriately, and denied entry to the country. Kala warned publicly: "if you identify as someone from the community, do not go to these Gulf countries."

sources.claim_summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Oman's criminalisation of same-sex activity and gender expression.

sources.title: Joint Stakeholder Submission to the UN Human Rights Council's 4th Universal Periodic Review on Trans Rights In Oman | Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute
sources.claim_summary: Cairo 52/White Tent joint UPR stakeholder report (Aug 2025) on trans rights in Oman: documents systemic legal and institutional discrimination - Article 266 of the Penal Code, the 'Rasd' surveillance unit monitoring and prosecuting non-conforming gender expression, prohibition of legal gender recognition and explicit ban on gender-affirming healthcare; Oman disregards prior UPR recommendations.

sources.title: Oman | Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute
sources.claim_summary: Cairo 52 country review of Oman: the 2018 Penal Code explicitly and implicitly criminalises trans expression and identity (Chapter 3); Royal Decree No. 75 (2019) prohibits healthcare practitioners from providing any gender-affirming care to trans people; legal gender recognition severely limited; cybercrime laws used to punish queer and trans expression.

sources.title: LGBT Rights in Oman: Laws, Penalties, and Restrictions - LegalClarity
sources.claim_summary: LegalClarity overview (June 2026): Oman criminalises all same-sex conduct (Articles 261-262 of the 2018 Penal Code, up to 3 years) and restricts gender expression, with consequences extending to foreign nationals (deportation on top of prison) and digital activity; prosecution generally requires a spouse/relative complaint unless a 'public scandal' occurred - an exception that swallows the rule.

sources.title: 'Made to remove shirt, touched inappropriately': Queer person alleges transphobia at Muscat airport
sources.claim_summary: The News Minute (Feb 2023): genderqueer/non-binary model and activist Nin Kala alleges a transphobic ordeal at Muscat airport - taken to an isolated room, made to remove her shirt twice 'for examination', touched inappropriately, and told to return to India despite a valid 10-day tourist visa.

HRW letter (July 2020) to Oman's Attorney General re: arrests and convictions under the 2018 Penal Code - four men arrested after photos from a private birthday party in Salalah circulated on Snapchat, convicted of 'immoral conduct', 'imitating the opposite sex' (Art. 266(d)) and cybercrime provisions; each sentenced to 3 years, a fine and street cleaning.

sources.title: Audacity in Adversity: LGBT Activism in the Middle East and North Africa | HRW
sources.claim_summary: HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - includes Oman's criminalisation and the annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across MENA.

Shafiqa Ahmadi, 'Islam and Homosexuality: Religious Dogma, Colonial Rule, and the Quest for Belonging' (Journal of Civil Rights and Economic Development, 2012): distinguishes homosexual acts from homosexual persons; in some Islamic countries acts are criminalised (even by death) while identity alone is not - scholarly context for Oman's legal-religious framework.
